guide.title: Douglaston, Queens: Douglas Manor, Douglaston Hill and Udalls Cove
guide.intro: Douglaston sits on a peninsula reaching into Little Neck Bay at the eastern edge of Queens. The city's planning table files it together with Little Neck as a single neighborhood tabulation area, QN1103, within Community District 11, and its ZIP codes are 11362 and 11363. Two New York City historic districts lie within it: the Douglaston Historic District, designated in 1997, and the Douglaston Hill Historic District, designated in 2004. The Landmarks Preservation Commission's register of individual landmarks lists two in Douglaston, the Cornelius Van Wyck House of about 1735 and the Benjamin P. Allen House of 1850, and both are private houses. Udalls Park Preserve runs from Northern Boulevard to Little Neck Bay, and Alley Pond Park borders the neighborhood on the west. Northern Boulevard runs through Douglaston, and Douglaston Parkway and Marathon Parkway carry Douglaston addresses.

sections.heading: Douglas Manor, Douglaston Hill and the two landmarks
sections.body:
The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the Douglaston Historic District in 1997, in a report describing "over 600 houses and some 150 related structures"; the city's PLUTO tax-lot file counts 638 lots inside the district's boundary. The Douglaston Hill Historic District followed in 2004, and the Commission's report for it counts thirty-one buildings; PLUTO counts thirty-one lots in the district and one more in its 2007 amendment. Wikipedia's National Register summary gives the National Register's Douglaston Hill district 83 contributing buildings and two contributing sites.

Douglas Manor was one of the Rickert-Finlay Realty Company's tracts. LP-1957 sets the firm's work out in one line: "Their projects included Norwood in Long Island City, Broadway-Flushing in Flushing, Bellcourt in Bayside, Douglas Manor in Douglaston, and Westmoreland in Little Neck."

The Cornelius Van Wyck House is one of the two individual landmarks. The 1966 designation entry gives it as "CORNELIUS VANWYCK HOUSE, 37-04 Douglaston Parkway (126 West Drive), Douglaston, Borough of Queens. Built about 1735, architect unknown. Landmark Site: Borough of Queens Tax Map Block 8056, Lot 62." PLUTO gives the same year. Of 5,583 PLUTO lots in ZIP codes 11362 and 11363, five carry a year built before 1900 — this house at 1735, 221 Arleigh Road and 236-12 Center Drive at 1850, 240-02 Poplar Street at 1850, and 231 Manor Road at 1870 — and the Van Wyck House is the earliest of them by 115 years. The Commission continued its public hearing on the designation to February 8, 1966, when four speakers spoke in favor, and the report records that "There were no speakers in opposition to designation at either meeting." PLUTO gives the owner as Van Wyck House, LLC and a single residential unit.

The Benjamin P. Allen House, also called the Allen-Beville House, stands at 29 Center Drive, the address in its LPC designation; PLUTO carries it as 236-12 Center Drive in ZIP 11363, built in 1850, with one residential unit and a private owner. The LPC dataset dates the designation to January 11, 1977, and the report's own header gives the landmark site as Block 8064, Lot 76. PLUTO also files the house inside the Douglaston Historic District.

The Wynant Van Zandt House at 600 West Drive is the Douglaston Club, and PLUTO gives the owner as Douglaston Club Inc. LP-1957 dates the house to 1819 with alterations after 1906, while PLUTO's year for the lot is 1931. It is a contributing building in the Douglaston Historic District rather than an individual landmark, and the club is private. The Commission's 1977 report on the Allen House records that William P. Douglas won national standing when his yacht Sappho defeated British challengers in the competition that has since become the America's Cup.

Zion Episcopal Church is at 243-20 Church Street, and the parish gives its mailing address as 243-01 Northern Boulevard. Its rectory at 242-02 44th Avenue is described in LP-2155 as nearly identical to a house inside the New York City Douglaston Hill Historic District, and the same sentence states the rectory is "not in the historic district." The church stands outside that district as well: both LP-2155 and LP-1957 state that "Zion Church is located outside the historic district," and LP-2155 records the new Zion Episcopal Church of 1924-25 as not located inside it either. Wikipedia's National Register summary lists Zion Episcopal Church of 1830 among the contributing buildings of the National Register's Douglaston Hill district.

LP-1957 identifies 216 Beverly Road as Alfred Scheffer's own house, and attributes the mansion at 1008 Shore Road to Buchman & Fox. It also records 233 Arleigh Road as the site of the Great White Oak. The tree was cut down in 2009.

sections.heading: The bay, the preserve and the parkway
sections.body:
Udalls Park Preserve is filed by NYC Parks as property Q452, 44.44 acres, in Community Board 11, and it has no street address; Parks gives its extent as "Northern Blvd., 244 St. to 247 St., Douglas Rd., Little Neck Bay." The cove it protects is shared ground. The Udalls Cove Preservation Committee writes that "Udalls Cove is an inlet of Little Neck Bay... between the Douglaston and Great Neck peninsulas," describes the Ravine as "a deep wooded gully that lies between Little Neck and Douglaston," and records that "Much of the area has been acquired by New York State and City, and the Village of Great Neck Estates."

The committee tells its own founding story this way: "Then one woman said, 'Enough.' Aurora Gareiss, a feisty, middle-aged Douglaston resident whose home looked out on Udalls Cove, determined that what was left of the wetlands and woods around the Cove should be conserved."

NYC Parks sets the local landforms out on its historical sign for the preserve: "These are the peninsulas of Great Neck, Bayside, and Douglaston that flank the pre-glacial river valley of Little Neck Bay and Udall's Cove." Alley Pond Park borders Douglaston on the west.

Catharine Turner Richardson Park is NYC Parks property Q059, 0.101 acres, in ZIP 11363, and it too has no street address; Parks gives its extent as "Douglaston Pkwy., Prospect Ave. bet. Poplar St. and Pine St." Douglaston Park Golf Course has its clubhouse at 63-20 Marathon Parkway, on a parcel PLUTO records as built in 1927 and owned by NYC Parks; PLUTO measures that tax lot at 50.0 acres, NYC Parks gives the golf course property as 104.6 acres, and the course reaches beyond the neighborhood.

The National Art League's gallery is at 44-21 Douglaston Parkway; the league gives its telephone as 718-224-3957 and lists a "95th Annual Online Juried Open Exhibition." The Immaculate Conception Center is at 72-45 Douglaston Parkway, held on the tax roll by Rocklyn Ecclesiastical Corp.; the center's own site describes over 80 acres, while PLUTO's tax lot for it measures 27.5 acres. Douglaston Plaza is at 242-02 61st Avenue. FDNY Engine 313 and Ladder 164 are quartered at 44-01 244th Street. Queens Public Library's Douglaston/Little Neck branch, named for both neighborhoods, is at 249-01 Northern Boulevard, and its North Hills branch is at 57-04 Marathon Parkway.

The Douglaston and Little Neck Historical Society serves both Douglaston and Little Neck. So does the Little Neck - Douglaston Memorial Day Parade Organization, Inc., whose route Wikipedia gives as running "from Great Neck to Douglaston Parkway along Northern Boulevard." Wikipedia records that Douglaston is "zoned for Benjamin N. Cardozo High School, in neighboring Bayside," and the NYPD's 111th Precinct serves the neighborhood from its station house at 45-06 215th Street, in Bayside.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Douglaston station on the Long Island Rail Road is at 235th Street and 41st Avenue. Wikipedia credits its 1962 station house to the architect Allan Gordon Lorimer.

Northern Boulevard runs through the neighborhood; the Douglaston and Little Neck Historical Society records that it was formerly Broadway. Douglaston Parkway carries addresses from the National Art League at 44-21 to the Immaculate Conception Center at 72-45. Marathon Parkway carries the Douglaston Park Golf Course clubhouse at 63-20 and the Queens Public Library's North Hills branch at 57-04. Douglaston shares its ZIP codes, 11362 and 11363, and its planning-table area, QN1103, with Little Neck.

Street names in Douglaston Hill have changed since LP-2155 was written: Pine Street is now 43rd Avenue, Poplar Street is now 42nd Avenue, Prospect Avenue is now 240th Street, and Willow Street is now Depew Avenue. NYC Parks describes Catharine Turner Richardson Park by the older names.

Within the Douglaston Historic District, West Drive, Shore Road, Arleigh Road, Beverly Road, Manor Road and Center Drive are residential streets that can be walked. The Douglas Manor shorefront is held in common by the Douglas Manor Association rather than as public parkland, and the Douglaston Club, the Cornelius Van Wyck House and the Benjamin P. Allen House are all private.

faq.question: How do I get to Douglaston?
faq.answer: Douglaston station on the Long Island Rail Road is at 235th Street and 41st Avenue; Wikipedia credits its 1962 station house to the architect Allan Gordon Lorimer. By road, Northern Boulevard runs through the neighborhood, and Douglaston Parkway and Marathon Parkway carry Douglaston addresses. The neighborhood is in Queens Community District 11, and its ZIP codes are 11362 and 11363.

faq.question: Which historic districts cover Douglaston?
faq.answer: Two New York City historic districts. The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the Douglaston Historic District in 1997, in a report describing "over 600 houses and some 150 related structures"; PLUTO counts 638 tax lots within its boundary. The Douglaston Hill Historic District followed in 2004, with thirty-one buildings counted in the Commission's report, and an amendment in 2007. Douglas Manor was one of the Rickert-Finlay Realty Company's tracts, listed in LP-1957 alongside Norwood in Long Island City, Broadway-Flushing in Flushing, Bellcourt in Bayside and Westmoreland in Little Neck.

faq.question: Is Zion Episcopal Church inside the historic district?
faq.answer: It depends which district. LP-2155 and LP-1957 both state that "Zion Church is located outside the historic district," and LP-2155 repeats it for the church of 1924-25 and for the rectory at 242-02 44th Avenue, which it calls "not in the historic district" — those are the New York City Douglaston Hill Historic District. Wikipedia's National Register summary lists Zion Episcopal Church of 1830 among the contributing buildings of the National Register's Douglaston Hill district. The church stands at 243-20 Church Street, with a mailing address at 243-01 Northern Boulevard.

faq.question: Which places in Douglaston are open to the public?
faq.answer: Udalls Park Preserve and Catharine Turner Richardson Park, both NYC Parks properties; Douglaston Park Golf Course, whose clubhouse is at 63-20 Marathon Parkway; the National Art League's gallery at 44-21 Douglaston Parkway; and the residential streets of the two historic districts. The Cornelius Van Wyck House and the Benjamin P. Allen House are single-family houses in private hands, the Douglaston Club at 600 West Drive is a private club, and the Douglas Manor shorefront is held in common by the Douglas Manor Association rather than as public parkland.

faq.question: Who laid out Douglaston Hill and named its streets?
faq.answer: LP-2155, of 2004, says that Van Beuren "sold it in 1843 to Jeremiah Lambertson, a local farmer, who held the property until 1853, when he laid it out in an urban grid, named the subdivision Marathon, and sold the lots at auction." LP-1957, of 1997, says that "William Douglas apparently attempted a suburban subdivision half a century earlier south of Douglas Manor" and that "He named a number of new streets after the abundant trees on his property (Pine, Poplar, Willow, Cherry)."

photos.title: Douglaston station from the Douglaston Parkway overpass
photos.description: The Long Island Rail Road platform runs along a wooded cut and curves out of sight to the west. A shingle-roofed station building with a clock and notice boards sits at the platform's edge, a blue sign reads "New York Platform," and an apartment tower rises on the ridge in the distance.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Cornelius Van Wyck House
places.summary: One of the two individual New York City landmarks in Douglaston, also addressed as 126 West Drive. The 1966 designation entry gives it as "CORNELIUS VANWYCK HOUSE, 37-04 Douglaston Parkway (126 West Drive), Douglaston, Borough of Queens. Built about 1735, architect unknown. Landmark Site: Borough of Queens Tax Map Block 8056, Lot 62." It is a single-family house in private hands, owned on the tax roll by Van Wyck House, LLC.
places.history: PLUTO gives the year built as 1735. Of 5,583 PLUTO lots in ZIP codes 11362 and 11363, five carry a year built before 1900, and this is the earliest of them by 115 years. The Landmarks Preservation Commission continued its public hearing on the designation to February 8, 1966, when four speakers spoke in favor; the report records that "There were no speakers in opposition to designation at either meeting."

places.name: Benjamin P. Allen House
places.summary: Also called the Allen-Beville House, and the second of Douglaston's two individual New York City landmarks. The address above is the one in its LPC designation; PLUTO carries the house as 236-12 Center Drive, in ZIP 11363, with one residential unit and a private owner. It is a private residence.
places.history: The LPC dataset dates the designation to January 11, 1977, and the report's own header gives the landmark site as Block 8064, Lot 76. PLUTO gives the year built as 1850 and files the house within the Douglaston Historic District.

places.name: Wynant Van Zandt House (Douglaston Club)
places.summary: The Wynant Van Zandt House, occupied by the Douglaston Club, whose name PLUTO gives as the owner of the lot: Douglaston Club Inc. It is a contributing building in the Douglaston Historic District rather than an individual landmark, and the club is private.
places.history: LP-1957 dates the house to 1819, with alterations after 1906. PLUTO's year built for the lot is 1931.

photos.title: Wynant Van Zandt House, occupied by the Douglaston Club
photos.description: A three-story white clapboard house with black shutters, a columned front porch under a striped awning and a railed stone stoop, photographed from the lawn on a clear winter day. Clipped shrubs line the foundation, a wreath hangs on the upper wall, and a lower clapboard wing continues to the right. The club is private.
photos.author: Peter Greenberg

places.name: Zion Episcopal Church
places.summary: An Episcopal parish church on Church Street; the parish gives its mailing address as 243-01 Northern Boulevard. It stands outside the New York City Douglaston Hill Historic District: LP-2155 and LP-1957 both state that "Zion Church is located outside the historic district." Wikipedia's National Register summary, describing a different district, lists Zion Episcopal Church of 1830 among the contributing buildings of the National Register's Douglaston Hill district.
places.history: LP-2155 records the new Zion Episcopal Church of 1924-25, and notes it as not located inside the City historic district.

photos.title: Zion Episcopal Church
photos.description: A white clapboard church with a tall louvred spire above a gabled front, seen through bare winter trees from the burial ground on its lawn. A wreath hangs over the entrance, a lower wing extends to the left, and headstones and a low rail stand in the grass in the foreground.
photos.author: Peter Greenberg

places.name: Zion Episcopal Church rectory
places.summary: The rectory of Zion Episcopal Church. LP-2155 describes it as nearly identical to a house inside the Douglaston Hill Historic District, and states in the same sentence that the rectory itself is "not in the historic district."

places.name: Douglaston Historic District
places.summary: A New York City historic district designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1997, covering Douglas Manor. LP-1957 describes "over 600 houses and some 150 related structures"; PLUTO counts 638 tax lots within the district's boundary. Its streets include West Drive, Shore Road, Arleigh Road, Beverly Road, Manor Road and Center Drive.
places.history: Douglas Manor was one of the Rickert-Finlay Realty Company's tracts. LP-1957 records that "Their projects included Norwood in Long Island City, Broadway-Flushing in Flushing, Bellcourt in Bayside, Douglas Manor in Douglaston, and Westmoreland in Little Neck."

places.name: Douglaston Hill Historic District
places.summary: A New York City historic district designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission in 2004, with an amendment in 2007. The Commission's report, LP-2155, counts thirty-one buildings in it; PLUTO counts thirty-one lots in the district and one more in the amendment. Zion Episcopal Church and its rectory both stand outside it.
places.history: LP-2155 records that Van Beuren "sold it in 1843 to Jeremiah Lambertson, a local farmer, who held the property until 1853, when he laid it out in an urban grid, named the subdivision Marathon, and sold the lots at auction." LP-1957 records that "William Douglas apparently attempted a suburban subdivision half a century earlier south of Douglas Manor" and that "He named a number of new streets after the abundant trees on his property (Pine, Poplar, Willow, Cherry)." The district's street names have since changed: Pine Street is now 43rd Avenue, Poplar Street is now 42nd Avenue, Prospect Avenue is now 240th Street, and Willow Street is now Depew Avenue.

places.name: Alfred Scheffer house
places.summary: A house in the Douglaston Historic District that LP-1957 identifies as Alfred Scheffer's own house. It is a private residence.

places.name: Buchman & Fox mansion, 1008 Shore Road
places.summary: A mansion on Shore Road in the Douglaston Historic District, attributed by LP-1957 to the architects Buchman & Fox. It is a private residence.

places.name: Site of the Great White Oak
places.summary: The Arleigh Road address that LP-1957 records as the site of the Great White Oak. The tree was cut down in 2009, and the address is a private property.

places.name: Udalls Park Preserve
places.summary: An NYC Parks preserve on Little Neck Bay, filed as property Q452 at 44.44 acres in Community Board 11. It has no street address; Parks gives its extent as "Northern Blvd., 244 St. to 247 St., Douglas Rd., Little Neck Bay." The Udalls Cove Preservation Committee writes that "Udalls Cove is an inlet of Little Neck Bay... between the Douglaston and Great Neck peninsulas," and describes the Ravine as "a deep wooded gully that lies between Little Neck and Douglaston."
places.history: The Udalls Cove Preservation Committee gives its own founding this way: "Then one woman said, 'Enough.' Aurora Gareiss, a feisty, middle-aged Douglaston resident whose home looked out on Udalls Cove, determined that what was left of the wetlands and woods around the Cove should be conserved." The committee records that "Much of the area has been acquired by New York State and City, and the Village of Great Neck Estates." NYC Parks' historical sign for the preserve reads: "These are the peninsulas of Great Neck, Bayside, and Douglaston that flank the pre-glacial river valley of Little Neck Bay and Udall's Cove."

places.name: Catharine Turner Richardson Park
places.summary: A small NYC Parks property, Q059, of 0.101 acres, in ZIP 11363. It has no street address; Parks gives its extent as "Douglaston Pkwy., Prospect Ave. bet. Poplar St. and Pine St." — the pre-renaming names for what are now 240th Street, 42nd Avenue and 43rd Avenue.

places.name: Douglaston Park Golf Course clubhouse
places.summary: The clubhouse end of Douglaston Park Golf Course, a municipal course. PLUTO records the parcel as owned by NYC Parks and built in 1927, and measures the tax lot at 50.0 acres; NYC Parks gives the golf course property as 104.6 acres. The course reaches beyond the neighborhood.

places.name: Douglaston station
places.summary: The Long Island Rail Road station serving the neighborhood, at 235th Street and 41st Avenue.
places.history: Wikipedia credits the 1962 station house to the architect Allan Gordon Lorimer.

places.name: National Art League
places.summary: An art league and gallery on Douglaston Parkway, listed on the tax roll under its own name. The league gives its telephone as 718-224-3957 and lists a "95th Annual Online Juried Open Exhibition."

places.name: Immaculate Conception Center
places.summary: A Roman Catholic center on Douglaston Parkway, held on the tax roll by Rocklyn Ecclesiastical Corp. The center's own site describes over 80 acres; PLUTO's tax lot for it measures 27.5 acres.

places.name: Douglaston Plaza
places.summary: A shopping center on 61st Avenue, held on the tax roll by Douglaston Shopping Center Owner LLC.

places.name: FDNY Engine 313 / Ladder 164
places.summary: The firehouse quartering FDNY Engine Company 313 and Ladder Company 164, on 244th Street.

places.name: Queens Public Library, Douglaston/Little Neck branch
places.summary: A Queens Public Library branch on Northern Boulevard, named for both Douglaston and Little Neck.

places.name: Queens Public Library, North Hills branch
places.summary: A Queens Public Library branch on Marathon Parkway.

entries.name: Douglaston Historic District
entries.note: Designated in 1997 over Douglas Manor. West Drive, Shore Road, Arleigh Road, Beverly Road, Manor Road and Center Drive are residential streets.

entries.name: Cornelius Van Wyck House
entries.note: 37-04 Douglaston Parkway, also addressed as 126 West Drive. Built about 1735, architect unknown, and a private single-family house.

entries.name: Benjamin P. Allen House
entries.note: 29 Center Drive, carried by PLUTO as 236-12 Center Drive. Built 1850 and designated an individual landmark on January 11, 1977. A private residence.

entries.name: Zion Episcopal Church
entries.note: 243-20 Church Street. LPC states the church stands outside the City's Douglaston Hill Historic District; the National Register district includes it.

entries.name: Udalls Park Preserve
entries.note: NYC Parks property Q452, 44.44 acres, running from Northern Boulevard to Little Neck Bay. Udalls Cove lies between the Douglaston and Great Neck peninsulas.

entries.name: Catharine Turner Richardson Park
entries.note: NYC Parks property Q059, 0.101 acres, on Douglaston Parkway at 240th Street between 42nd Avenue and 43rd Avenue.

entries.name: National Art League
entries.note: 44-21 Douglaston Parkway. The league lists a "95th Annual Online Juried Open Exhibition" and gives its telephone as 718-224-3957.

entries.name: Douglaston Park Golf Course clubhouse
entries.note: 63-20 Marathon Parkway. PLUTO records the parcel as built in 1927 and owned by NYC Parks; the course reaches beyond the neighborhood.

entries.name: Douglaston station
entries.note: The Long Island Rail Road station at 235th Street and 41st Avenue. Wikipedia credits the 1962 station house to Allan Gordon Lorimer.

links.note: Douglaston is zoned for Benjamin N. Cardozo High School in neighboring Bayside, and the NYPD's 111th Precinct serves it from 45-06 215th Street there.
